The nerve cell body lies in the brain, spinal cord or dorsal or ventral root ganglion of spinal cord. In the brain or spinal cord, it is difficult to make out the difference between dendrites and axons on the basis of their length. The presence of the sheath helps us to find out the difference. But most of them are non-myelinated cells. We know that the nerve cell is the structural and functional unit of nervous system. Our nervous system consists of more than100 billion of them, which communicate with each other in a specific manner. Dendrites of one nerve cell connect to the axons of the other nerve cell through connections called as a ‘synapse’. Fig-4: Synapse Synapse Synapse is the functional region of contact between two neurons, where information from one neuron is transmitted or relayed to another neuron. Though these are regions of minute gaps and essentially neurons do not have any protoplasmic connection between them yet information is passed from one nerve cell to the other through these gaps either in the form of chemical or electrical signals or both. These synapses are mainly found usually in the brain, spinal cord and around the spinal cord. Beyond these areas the axon carries the signals from brain and spinal cord to respective parts of our body. 104 Coordination 5.4 Pathways: From stimulus to response In the holding stick activity you observed that there is coordination between eye and fingers. Different pathways are taken by nerves to bring about this coordinated activity. On the basis of pathways followed, nerves are classified mainly into three different types. They are as follows. (A) Afferent nerves or Sensory nerves : The nerves which carry messages towards the central nervous system (spinal cord or brain) from nerve endings on the muscles of different sense organs are called afferent or sensory nerves. (B) Efferent nerves or motor nerves : The nerves which carry messages from the central nervous system to body parts that shall carry out the response to effector muscles are called efferent or motor nerves. (C) Association nerves (Interneurons) : These nerves link together the afferent and efferent nerves in central nervous system (brain and spinal cord). x Which organs of your body were the detector and effector in Activity-1? x How do you think are the information carried on the afferent and efferent nerves (Give answer with respect to activity-1)? (AS7) 100 Coordination Everyday we do many activities such as sharpening of a pencil, grasping a door knob, walking or running, driving, and a few physical actions. All these actions involve well coordinated movements made with well balanced postures. In fact, whenever we move some basic functions such as movement, balance and coordination work together in performing motions of body parts. Even standing upright is a challenge of balancing on just two feet with a narrow base. Yet, it is common for us not only to stand upright easily and apparently, effortlessly, but also while keeping our balance to perform many functions like walking, running etc. x What other functions do you think are needed in coordination and balance? All our functions are carried out by an effort of several systems working together. For example, while movement, we hardly ever use just the skeletal system or muscular system alone, several other systems also have their own roles to play. Even within the muscular system, several muscles work in a systamatic manner. x What triggers the movement of the muscles? All our body parts, mainly the tissues and cells in them work by picking up signals of change (also called as stimuli) from their surroundings. They then respond to them. This process triggers different functions in our body. For example, it is natural to move to a side of the road when we hear or see a car approaching. Chapter Coordination 101 Coordination x How do we respond so fast to a situation? 5.1 Responding to stimuli x What helps us to respond to such signals of change? x Why does the living body respond to such signals? All living organisms respond to stimuli. Changes in the surroundings or signals of changes or stimulus are reasons for responses by living organisms. The cat may be running because it saw a mouse. Plants grow towards the sunlight. We start sweating when the surroundings are hot and humid. The ability to react to particular stimulus in a particular situation must be of great importance in ensuring the survival of the organism. There is a sequence of events that brings about responses. They start from detecting a change in outer or inner environment of the body or stimuli, then transmission of the information is the second stage, processing of the same is the third stage and execution of the appropriate action is last stage. parsed_output.answer: A synapse is the functional region of contact between two neurons where information is transmitted from one neuron to another. It is a gap across which signals are passed either in the form of chemical or electrical signals. When a stimulus is received by the dendrites of a neuron, it sets off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse. This impulse is transmitted through the cell body and axon. The chemicals from the axon cross the synapse and reach the next neuron, allowing the transfer of information across the nervous system.
